entry.title: fix(serve): every build door asks for words, since none means to ask …
entry.content:
fix(serve): every build door asks for words, since none means to ask for none

Buying a recording's second part rebuilt the whole reader with no word a
reader could tap, the first part's marks included. The part and chapter
doors write their own job options and never carried `words`, and
`Library._builder` read `difficulty=bool(options.get("words"))`, so
`Pipeline.annotate` returned None, every section shipped an empty word
table, and the job said `done`. The two chat doors had forgotten the same
key the day before (8b4cf17); a third door had too, as that fix predicted.

`_builder` now reads `options.get("words", True)`: on unless a door says
otherwise, and nothing anywhere says otherwise. The default lives where
every door meets, so the next door cannot forget. Pinned on the part door,
the chapter door, a bare build, and an explicit opt-out.

A deploy runs `rebuild --words` over every home, so affected readers get
their marks back on the box without a hand.

entry.title: feat(reader): a way to disagree with the offer, and nothing more
entry.content:
feat(reader): a way to disagree with the offer, and nothing more

The served next text (targum-internal#176) offers one text with a stated reason
and no way to say "not that one". Its open decision 4 asked whether a refusal
should exist, and 2026-09-09 answered: a quiet "something else" link that draws
again, with no memory.

Not a refusal the server remembers. The whole argument for the served text is
that saying yes costs nothing; a refusal that remembered would turn a door into
a profile nobody asked to build, and drag in decay, undo and a per-reader store.
Drawing again costs a click and removes the only bad feeling the single door
has, which is being told what to read with no way to disagree except leaving.

`next_after` returns a short list rather than one pick. The page fetches nothing
— the rule in CLAUDE.md, pinned by test_render.py — so a refusal cannot ask the
library for another text, and the alternatives ride in the page.

**Every draw keeps the reason that is true of it.** A pick from the wider pool
still says it is a different Hebrew on the second draw; one below this text says
it is easier rather than pretending to be a step up. A refusal that lied about
what it was offering would be worse than no refusal. That needed one new
sentence, "Easier than this one.", and a band: five points, which is roughly the
width of one of the library's own levels.

The control is rendered only where there is a second pick and takes itself away
when the list runs out, because one that offers for ever is offering nothing.

Closes DLangellotti/targum-internal#233

entry.title: fix(licences): a targum is two texts, and the report was reading one
entry.content:
fix(licences): a targum is two texts, and the report was reading one

`targum licences` built its rows as `("text", entry.id, entry.licence)` and never
looked at `entry.translations`. But the English beside the Hebrew is a separate
work under a separate licence, recorded per translation since #115, and it ships
in the same reader.

Measured on the catalogue: 502 entries, 131 translations, and **90 of those
translations stand worse than the source they sit beside** — 88 free-in-Hebrew
against owed-in-English, and two with nothing recorded at all. None of them were
counted, so "451 nothing owed" was short by 88.

Nothing was closed. No NonCommercial or NoDerivatives translation was hiding
behind a Public Domain source, so no door the report called open was actually
shut. What was wrong is the bookkeeping, and the bookkeeping is the point of
#115: an obligation nobody has written down is one nobody will honour.

So: every translation is a row, and a line under the table names the pairs whose
two halves disagree, which is the number somebody preparing an export needs and
neither column showed. `unknown` ranks above `owed` in that comparison on
purpose — this command's own rule is that an unchecked licence is not an absent
one.

`scripts/backfill_licences.py` learns the same. A Sefaria rendering names its
language in the ref (`sefaria:en:Ruth`) and the Hebrew side does not, which is
the only difference between the two readers; asked of Ruth's English it returns
the CC-BY that was recorded there by hand.

Closes DLangellotti/targum-internal#234

Sefaria answers to `Mesilat Yesharim` and to `Mesillat Yesharim`, and its index

to the Tanakh default:

    Sefaria has no 'Tanach with Ta'amei Hamikra' of Mesillat Yesharim.

Which reads like a missing book rather than a missing pin, about a book that is
there — 898 blocks and 30,620 vocalized Hebrew words, paired segment for segment
with an English that covers all of it.

fix(catalogue): a cover prompt for the new kind, which the Draw button needs

`cover_prompt` maps every `Kind` to a phrase, and a value missing from it raises
`KeyError` out of the `/cover` route — which is what happened to the scenes, and
is why `tests/test_public.py` pins every value. CI caught it; the local run did

Said as the hour rather than as an object: the brand rules below already refuse
ritual objects of any tradition, and what a prayer book actually is to a reader
is the morning it is opened at.

entry.title: feat(catalogue): Kind.liturgy, because a siddur is not a document
entry.content:
feat(catalogue): Kind.liturgy, because a siddur is not a document

The siddur is the most-read Hebrew text in the world and the best one on this
shelf to learn from, for a reason none of the others can claim: it is the same
words in the same order every morning, which is spaced repetition already
installed in a reader's life. `Kind` had no word for it. `document` would have
been the shrug, and `Kind` exists so a reader is told what they are holding.

Decided deliberately rather than defaulted, which is what
targum-internal#120 asked for. It also gives the Beit Midrash mode that
`JEWISH = {tanakh, judaica}` already anticipates something to hang on: a text
being *recited* wants the Hebrew first, the translation second, and a gloss that
stops repeating itself by the tenth morning. None of that is buildable off
`document`.

The library page gets "Prayer" and a note. Its chips are drawn from what is
actually on the shelf, so nothing appears until a liturgy text is filed.

And a test that every `Kind` and `Register` has a word beside it, because
`named()` returns "" for a value it does not know: a new enum value shows as a
blank column and no filter, and says nothing about it. `Register.none` is
excluded — it is the empty string for texts that are not in Hebrew.

Refs DLangellotti/targum-internal#120

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: chore: a pre-push hook checks the private half, which nothing else could
entry.content:
chore: a pre-push hook checks the private half, which nothing else could

Eight gitignored modules — the weekly's writer and voice, the dialogue writer,
the recording cutter and aligner — exist only in the main checkout. CI has a
public checkout, a worktree of a tracked branch carries no ignored files, and
the wheel does not carry them either: hatchling drops VCS-ignored files, and
`[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel].artifacts` adds back exactly one, verified by
unzipping the wheel tonight's deploy shipped. So no lint, no type check and no
test saw them, while they go on depending on the public half — a rename in
`recording/`, `weekly/index.py` or `models.py` breaks one with every check still
green, and the failure surfaces at the next weekly build, by hand, days later.

A push is the right moment. It is when a public-half change stops being local,
and the last moment the two halves are in front of each other, because what goes
to GitHub is only ever one of them.

The hook runs ruff, ruff format, mypy and `tests/test_private_half.py` over the
eight. In a tree that has none of them it is silent and instant, which is every
worktree; a tree with *some* of them is refused, because a partial private half
builds a wheel with holes in it. `--no-verify` skips it.

Not committed into `.git/hooks` because that is per-clone by design, so
`deploy/hooks/install.sh` puts it there and `CLAUDE.md` names both beside the
by-hand command.

Installing it immediately found three lint errors and a formatting divergence
sitting in the private half, on top of the three found by hand the same day; and
a deliberate rename of `weekly.models.dated_title` was caught twice over, by
mypy and by the import test.

Closes DLangellotti/targum-internal#230

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: perf(serve): the line is answered by the line, not by everything ever…
entry.content:
perf(serve): the line is answered by the line, not by everything ever run

`Library.mine` computed a reader's place in the queue by filtering the whole job
registry — every job the process knows about, loaded at startup from every row
ever written. Since 2026-09-05 every chat turn is a job row, which is right and
is how the spending rails see a turn, so that registry grows with every turn
anybody takes and a question about the two builds waiting was being answered by
walking the conversations.

`Jobs` is a dict that indexes the builds as they arrive, and `Jobs.waiting`
returns the ones worth answering about — sweeping out, on the way past, exactly
what `mine` would have skipped: settled for longer than `RECENT_MS`, or gone
from the registry by any route. That is one condition rather than two policies
to keep in step.

The index is maintained inside the dict rather than at the thirteen places that
assign a job, because an index the caller has to remember is an index that
drifts; `Library.jobs`'s setter wraps a plain mapping so the tests that stage a
queue by assigning a whole dict keep it.

What the server *remembers* is deliberately unchanged: every job is still in the
registry, `/job/<id>` still answers about one from three months ago, and the
ledger on disk is still the record. Only the per-request cost moves. Bounding
the memory is the other half of targum-internal#231 and stays filed.

Refs DLangellotti/targum-internal#231
